statement: Different whole numbers are chosen from 1 to 20. What is the smallest number of them you must choose to be sure that two of the chosen numbers differ by exactly 5?

choices.misconception: I sorted the numbers into 5 groups by their remainder on division by 5 and said 6 numbers force two into one group, but two numbers in a group can differ by 10 or 15.
I found that 10 numbers can be chosen with no two differing by 5 and gave 10, forgetting that the answer is one more than that.
I counted the 15 pairs of numbers from 1 to 20 that differ by 5 and thought I needed one more number than there are pairs.
I sorted the numbers into 5 groups by their remainder on division by 5 and answered with the number of groups.

hints: How many numbers can you choose while still avoiding a difference of 5?
Make boxes so that two numbers in the same box always differ by exactly 5. Count the boxes to see when two chosen numbers must share one, and find a big set that avoids it.

solutions.reliable: First, 10 numbers are not enough: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 has no two numbers differing by 5 (differences inside each block are at most 4, and between blocks at least 6). Next, any 11 numbers work. Split 1 to 20 into the ten pairs (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 8), (4, 9), (5, 10), (11, 16), (12, 17), (13, 18), (14, 19), (15, 20), which use every number exactly once. With 11 numbers in 10 pairs, some pair has both of its numbers chosen, and they differ by 5. So the answer is 11. The transferable idea: for a 'be sure' question, find the largest set that avoids the event; the answer is one more, and pigeonhole boxes prove it.
solutions.elegant: Think in chains where neighbours differ by 5: (1, 6, 11, 16), (2, 7, 12, 17), and so on, five chains of 4. From a chain of 4 you can take at most 2 numbers without taking neighbours, so at most $5 \times 2 = 10$ numbers avoid a difference of 5, and an 11th always creates one.

whyOnTest: Tests the pigeonhole principle with well-chosen boxes, pairs that differ by 5, plus an example showing one fewer is not enough.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
